titleStmt.title: No. 942
The Ambassador in Jordan (Mallory) to the Department of State

div.head:
No. 942
The Ambassador in Jordan (Mallory) to the Department of State
div.p:
Top Secret
Limited Distribution Alpha

list.item: Approach to Settlement of Palestine Problem

div.p: The Department’s very interesting instruction on an approach to settlement of the Arab-Israel problem has been read with high interest. It is germane and timely. Due to a series of circumstances, a reply was not prepared prior to the Regional Economic Conference for the Near East held at the American Embassy in Damascus on December 14–16. At that meeting, an extensive discussion of the Palestine problem took place. Possible approaches in general, specific inhibiting factors and problems in individual countries were reviewed. Because of that discussion, participated in by Ambassador George Allen, this reply will be brief. With respect to any approach at this time, it is believed that an effort may well be made during the next six months. With the settlement of attention-catching disputes in other places, failure to approach this one which now looms so acute would raise questions on the sincerity of our motives and on the quality of our international leadership.

There are certain minima which are precedent to a successful outcome. Some should be devised or contrived before an approach is made; some should be ascertained in advance, or at least estimates made. As viewed from Jordan, they are:
(1) Determination or taking the risk that Israel will, in fact, conclude peace;
(2) Realization by Israel that she must agree to the principle of repatriation even realizing that few, if any, Arabs would return and remain in Israel;
(3) Some sort of compensation for Arab properties;
(4) Promote and engender Egyptian leadership in the matter, even to the extent of pushing her to a separate position in the Arab world;
(5) A determined and coordinated course of action on the part of the United Kingdom and the United States, and the virtual exclusion of the French.
These are mostly self-explanatory and self-evident. In addition, there are matters which could greatly help in concluding a settlement even though they might not be indispensable. They are:

list.item: (a) Progress on the negotiations for the unified development of the Jordan Basin. Such progress would assist in the settlement and should be undertaken prior to the general approach. Knowledge that a general approach were to be undertaken might result in holding off in order to use the Unified Plan as a pawn in the bargaining.
(b) The adherence of Iraq to the Turkish-Pakistan Pact. The indirect effect of this move on the members of the Arab League should be wholesome.

(c) Quiet on the Israeli-Jordan borders. It would be most desirable that Israel be informed that acts of armed forces or armed retaliation will be viewed severely—perhaps in a financial sense. Moreover, the Israeli posture on the border may be carefully watched during negotiations as an earnest of good intentions of Israel, which has been known to stir up the border just as the Arabs were about to take a constructive step.

div.p: With respect to timing, it is desirable that the negotiations of Ambassador Eric Johnston proceed even decision with the British of a timetable [sic]. That much probably would become known to the Israeli Government. Certainly there should be no thought of approaches to any government on this matter until after Ambassador Johnston has given the Arabs and the Israelis an opportunity to accept international cooperation or to refuse it. Further, it would be desirable to wait for a few months or at least wait until the Spring of 1955 in the hope that Turkish discussion with the Iraqis may result in adherence of Iraq to the Turkish-Pakistan axis. At that time it would be desirable to again scan the troubled Palestinian horizon for a timetable.

As far as Jordan is concerned, inducements either of the carrot or the stick type are not likely to be of much avail. The Jordanians are concerned primarily with questions of principle, face, and hurt pride, and economic or military aid granted or withheld would not loom large in their evaluation. Indirect influence with the British certainly would be stronger than from the United States directly but that alone does not suffice. Some public indication that Israel might have just perchance been slightly wrong at some time would be of far more value than large sums of aid. With respect to financial aid, per se, quite apart from the influence it might have on Israeli
public opinion, the Jordanians (at least, the daily press) would be quite as happy to see aid to Israel reduced as for Jordan to receive it. Inducements to a settlement are primary points (2) and (3) mentioned above as precedent. All others fall into a secondary and more negotiable category. There are indications that some of the principal leaders of Jordanian political life are becoming weary of the present situation and have expressed privately the realization that some end or settlement must eventually ensue. Always, however, there is in the background, either voiced or taken for granted, that repatriation must be recognized and compensation given.
With respect to the specific objectives cited in the reference instruction, my reaction is as follows:

1. This appears sound. If there is to be any peace ever, it must be between Jordan and Israel. Leading to that peace, Egypt could be and probably should be the primary mover and force. In that connection, such matters as economic or grant military assistance which would have little influence in Jordan might be of importance to Egypt. With Egypt–Jordan–Israel more or less concurring, it is felt that Jordan would welcome Lebanon’s participation.

2. Permanent recognized boundaries for Israel will be a difficult pill for Jordan to swallow, but it is implicit in any form of peace and can probably be arrived at. There will need to be certain frontier rectifications.

3. The problem of security on the border and control of infiltration has an inflated value in the eyes of the protagonists. If there is supposed to be a peace arrangement, both sides should be willing to forget the problem of infiltration and accept a certain amount of crossing and sheep stealing as fulfillment of the remark by the Frenchman that human nature is still very prevalent.

4. Termination of the Suez Canal blockade and of the Arab secondary boycott can likewise be achieved. Should we not also seek termination of the Arab primary boycott? Certainly it should be a considerable inducement to Israel to have Arab markets open for her produce and transit trade and, likewise, Jordan should welcome (even though she may not promptly realize the advantage of) the Israeli market for agricultural products from the Jordan Valley. This could, of course, come at a later date.
5. This has elsewhere been discussed.
6. This has elsewhere been discussed.

7. I am not sure what is meant by this caption. Other Arab States apparently would be glad to have Jerusalem internationalized, but Jordan would not. It happens that the Old City of Jerusalem is a part of Jordan under the sovereignty of its King. This doesn’t mean so much to the Jerusalemite, especially the Christian inhabitants, but I can foresee no successful negotiation for peace which attempts in any way to divide Jerusalem from the Kingdom of Jordan. Such being the case, there would appear to be no place for an international authority limited to the holy places. The holy places are pretty much in the Old City, unless one includes Nazareth, parts of Galilee, etc., and this is probably not meant.

The weapons ban is worthwhile if the Israelis will agree to it together with United Nations supervision and inspection on Mt. Scopus which the Jordanians now feel, probably correctly, has been fortified. Mt. Scopus, be it not forgotten, is the key to the tactical situation of the whole of the Jerusalem area.
8. Desirable.

9. As pointed out above, it is desirable that agreement on the unified development of the Jordan Valley be achieved before overall negotiations. If not, then it should form a part of the over-all peace since an old-fashioned water fight could break out at any time. It need not be a condition precedent to settlement, but its absence certainly could be a disturbing factor.

With respect to the final point on page 2 of the Department’s instruction, it would be fruitful to achieve progress on area defense arrangements and a series of bilaterals linking certain Arab States. Turkey and Pakistan deserve primary consideration. This is from the positive standpoint. If Egypt can be brought along not to oppose such arrangements, it will be desirable. On the negative approach, Arab activity looking towards implementation or reinforcement of their common defense mechanism should be frustrated as it can only be an impediment to our larger aims.

The Department’s tentative thinking that the best tactics would be a combination of a present step-by-step approach with an across-the-board effort would appear to be the only one at this time. It must be realized that there have not been many steps, and those have been purely within the field of policy decisions by the United States. We do not appear to have succeeded in causing any steps to be taken by either Israel or the Arabs. Nevertheless the improved, if still unspoken, attitude extant may be considered part of this approach. An across-the-board arrangement in combination with the British will be desirable although the actual negotiating techniques may require a long series of steps and bargainings. In this respect, it is to be recalled that although the word is nowadays applied primarily to the Jew that the Arab is also a Semite.

It is agreed that the first approach should be to Egypt. In this respect I believe Egypt’s demonstrated determination in dealing with the Moslem Brotherhood in the face of dismay and reluctance in other parts of the Arab world may well promote a position of Egyptian leadership and determination. There are those who judge that, on the contrary, Egypt may feel that having gone so far in the Moslem Brotherhood matter, she would not wish soon to again earn Arab displeasure. My personal experience with dictatorial-type governments would lead me to place credence in the former interpretation.

Concerning tactics, the Trieste technique would appear as appropriate as any. Certainly direct contact with Israel cannot be made
by Jordanians—that is, if they wish to be alive the next morning. Even the Trieste technique poses problems for the Jordan Government and will probably increase the peril to the Prime Minister’s life. Indirect negotiations through either the United States or Great Britain would arouse too many troubles to be entertained. Probably approaches to individual Arab countries would be preferable to simultaneous approaches to two or more of them. However, it would seem that if the initial approach is to Egypt and Israel appeared at all fruitful then Jordan should be brought into the matter fairly promptly. It might also be desirable to bring Lebanon in subsequently, especially if it appeared that she might be a moderating influence. If Egypt would move towards a settlement, her example and leadership would be very important. Jordan dares not move alone or initially, but possible might follow Egyptian leadership. The question of timing as set forth appears a little too soon and a little too precise. As previously indicated, it should be delayed for the Unified Plan and Iraqi defense discussions.

There would not appear to be inducements which might be offered by the United States or the United Kingdom to Jordan. Those inducements must come from Israeli willingness to move. Assurance of a longer term aid program would be some inducement, but it must be supplement to, and could not replace, the matters of principle.

With specific regard to Jordan, I do not see that moving forward simultaneously on area defense arrangements would be of much assistance. It might be of help with respect to Egypt, Iraq, etc. However, the negative effect of movement toward a common Arab defense scheme could be of importance and should be avoided.
